prompt: On the course's Ubuntu server, `logging_collector` is off. Who put the server's standard error into /var/log/postgresql/postgresql-16-main.log?
hint: Look at how the unit starts the cluster.

choices.text: The logger process the server starts at boot
choices.why: That process exists only with logging_collector = on, and it writes under the data directory.

choices.text: systemd's journal, which forwards each line to the file
choices.why: The journal held only the unit starting; the server's lines never went through it.

choices.text: logrotate, which creates the file every week
choices.why: logrotate cuts the file; it does not decide where the server writes.

choices.text: pg_ctlcluster, through pg_ctl -l
choices.why: Right. pg_ctl -l opens the file and hands it to the postmaster as standard error, and every backend inherits it.

prompt: Why did `SELECT pg_current_logfile();` return nothing on the default Ubuntu server, though a log file plainly exists?
hint: Which files does it know about?

choices.text: ana lacks the privilege to see the path
choices.why: ana is a superuser. After jsonlog was turned on, the same query from the same role returned a path.

choices.text: It reports only files the server opened itself
choices.why: Right. With the collector off, the file was opened by pg_ctl, so the server has nothing to report.

choices.text: The log was empty at that moment
choices.why: The file had start-up lines in it, 560 bytes. Its size is not what the function looks at.

choices.text: The function needs log_destination = 'csvlog'
choices.why: It answered for jsonlog too. What it needs is the collector writing the file.

prompt: You inherit a server and `/var/log/postgresql/postgresql-16-main.log` ends with "redirecting log output to logging collector process" from three weeks ago. What do you conclude?
hint: Read the HINT line that follows it.

choices.text: The server has been quiet for three weeks
choices.why: That is the trap: the log moved, and this file stopped growing on the day it did.

choices.text: Logging is broken and the server is writing nothing
choices.why: The line says where it went, not that it stopped.

choices.text: The log moved to the collector's files
choices.why: Right. Every line since then is in the collector's files, by default in log/ inside the data directory.

choices.text: logrotate has moved the newer lines into a .1 file
choices.why: Rotation keeps the newest lines in the current file. The redirect line is the server's own.

prompt: With `log_line_prefix = '%m [%p] %q%u@%d '`, why does a checkpoint line end right after `[103]`?
hint: One escape prints nothing at all.

choices.text: %q, for processes with no session
choices.why: Right. The checkpointer has no user or database, so everything after %q is left out for it.

choices.text: Background processes ignore log_line_prefix
choices.why: They use it: the time and [103] come from %m and %p.

choices.text: The checkpointer runs as postgres, and that name is hidden
choices.why: Nothing is hidden by name. It has no role or database to print.

choices.text: %u and %d print only after a reload
choices.why: The client lines in the same file carried ana@shop without any reload.

prompt: No statement logging was configured, yet `SELECT 1/0;` left a `STATEMENT:` line after the `ERROR:`. Which parameter wrote it?
hint: Its default is error.

choices.text: log_statement
choices.why: It was none, as the first query of the lesson showed.

choices.text: log_min_messages
choices.why: That decides which severities are written, not whether the failing statement follows the error.

choices.text: log_min_error_statement
choices.why: Right. Any statement that fails at error or above is written after its error message.

choices.text: log_line_prefix, through %q
choices.why: The prefix shapes the start of each line; it adds no lines.

prompt: To see which program sent each statement, the course added the escape ___ to the end of log_line_prefix.
hint: It prints application_name.

prompt: A log shipper parses lines with a regular expression written for `%m [%p] %q%u@%d `. Somebody adds `%h` in the middle of the prefix on a busy server. What is the likely result?
hint: Who depends on the prefix's shape?

choices.text: The server refuses the new prefix until a restart
choices.why: log_line_prefix changes on a reload, and the reload itself is logged with the new value.

choices.text: Lines stop matching the shipper's pattern
choices.why: Right. Every tool that reads the log is written against the prefix, so changing its format breaks the parser.

choices.text: Nothing, because %h is empty for local connections
choices.why: It prints [local] for socket connections, and anyway the layout of the line has changed.

choices.text: Old lines in the file are rewritten in the new format
choices.why: A log is appended to; nothing rewrites what was already written.

prompt: Match each parameter to the line it adds to the log.
hint: Each one writes only when its event happens.

pairs.right: still waiting for ShareLock … after 1000 ms

prompt: With `log_min_duration_statement = '50ms'`, the full scan of orders was logged and `SELECT name FROM customers WHERE id = 42` was not. Why is that the behaviour you want?
hint: What would the log be if every statement went in?

choices.text: Only the slow ones are worth reading; the rest would bury them
choices.why: Right. A threshold keeps the log to the statements worth a look instead of the millions that were fine.

choices.text: Statements by primary key are never worth logging
choices.why: One that took two seconds would be worth it, and the threshold would catch it.

choices.text: The lookup was answered from cache and never executed
choices.why: It executed and returned Customer 42; it was simply under 50 ms.

choices.text: Logging it would have needed log_statement = 'all'
choices.why: A threshold of 0 would log it too. The point is that 50 ms chose not to.

prompt: In the lock-wait lines, what does `DETAIL: Process holding the lock: 254. Wait queue: 258.` let you do that pg_stat_activity may not, an hour later?
hint: pg_stat_activity shows only what is happening now.

choices.text: Find what 254 was running, by grepping [254]
choices.why: Right. The pid in the prefix ties the blocker's own lines to the waiter's, after both sessions are gone.

choices.text: Kill process 254 from the log
choices.why: The log records; it acts on nothing. And an hour later 254 is probably gone.

choices.text: Prove a deadlock happened
choices.why: This was a plain wait that ended with acquired ShareLock; a deadlock has its own ERROR line.

choices.text: Raise deadlock_timeout for process 258 alone
choices.why: That is a setting, not something the log line enables, and it would only delay the line.

prompt: Which logging parameter did the course find already on, by default, in PostgreSQL 16?
hint: It writes a starting and a complete line.

choices.text: log_connections
choices.why: It was off; the lesson turned it on to see the three arrival lines.

choices.text: log_lock_waits
choices.why: It was off until the lesson set it.

choices.text: log_autovacuum_min_duration at 0
choices.why: Its default is 600000 ms, ten minutes, which on most servers logs nothing.

choices.text: log_checkpoints
choices.why: Right. PostgreSQL 16 turned it on by default.

prompt: Over a week, most `checkpoint starting:` lines on a server say `wal` rather than `time`. What does that tell you?
hint: What starts a checkpoint other than the clock?

choices.text: Somebody is running CHECKPOINT by hand
choices.why: A manual one said immediate force wait, as in the lab.

choices.text: WAL fills up before the timeout
choices.why: Right. The server ran out of WAL room before the clock said so, which is lesson 8's question about max_wal_size.

choices.text: WAL archiving is failing
choices.why: Nothing in the reason word says anything about archiving.

choices.text: The log is being written to the WAL
choices.why: The server log and the write-ahead log are unrelated files.

prompt: With `log_statement = 'all'`, 10,000 pgbench transactions grew the log by 8758557 bytes. About how many bytes is that per transaction? (Give a whole number.)
hint: Divide.

prompt: Why did logcost.sh report that the log grew by 0 bytes before log_statement was changed?
hint: What does each remaining parameter wait for?

choices.text: pgbench writes to its own log, not the server's
choices.why: The next run, with log_statement = 'all', grew the server's log by megabytes with pgbench's statements.

choices.text: The log had just been rotated and stat read the new file
choices.why: Rotation came later in the lesson; both stat calls read the same file.

choices.text: No statement was slow, waited for a lock or spilled
choices.why: Right. Those parameters write only when their event happens, and none of the 70,000 statements triggered one.

choices.text: The server buffers log lines and flushes them at checkpoints
choices.why: Lines are written as they happen; the next run showed the growth at once.

prompt: An auditor asks to know whenever a table is created, altered or dropped. Which setting answers that and can stay on for good?
hint: One value of log_statement records only schema changes.

choices.text: log_statement = 'all'
choices.why: It records those, and every other statement as well: gigabytes a day and every literal in plain text.

choices.text: log_min_duration_statement = 0
choices.why: That logs every statement with its duration, which is even more bytes than 'all'.

choices.text: log_statement = 'ddl'
choices.why: Right. It writes every CREATE, ALTER and DROP, a handful of lines a week on most servers.

choices.text: log_lock_waits = on, since ALTER takes a lock
choices.why: It logs only waits longer than deadlock_timeout; most ALTERs would never appear.

prompt: Order these severities by how much they took down with them, least first.
hint: One statement, one session, the whole server.
trap: FATAL sounds like the end of everything, and it is one session.

prompt: A FATAL line appears: `password authentication failed for user "report"`. What stopped?
hint: Read the severity table, not the word's mood.

choices.text: The whole server, which must be restarted
choices.why: That is PANIC. FATAL ends one session.

choices.text: Every session of the role report
choices.why: Other sessions of report are untouched; the line is about one attempt.

choices.text: The statement report was running
choices.why: A failed statement is ERROR. This one failed at the door.

choices.text: One connection attempt
choices.why: Right. FATAL ends one session; here the session never began.

prompt: Ubuntu's logrotate configuration for the PostgreSQL log uses `copytruncate`. Why not simply rename the file?
hint: Who holds the file open, and can it be told to reopen it?

choices.text: Renaming needs the server stopped
choices.why: A rename works on an open file; the problem is where the writes go afterwards.

choices.text: copytruncate compresses the file at the same time
choices.why: Compression is compress and delaycompress, separate lines of the same file.

choices.text: It loses no lines, unlike renaming
choices.why: It is the one that can: lines written between the copy and the truncation land in neither file.

choices.text: The server would keep writing into the renamed file
choices.why: Right. It holds the file as standard error and cannot be told to reopen it, so the contents are copied and the original emptied.

prompt: Why did switching to `log_destination = 'jsonlog'` need `logging_collector = on` and a restart?
hint: Which process can write a format other than plain text?

choices.text: jsonlog needs the jq package on the server
choices.why: jq only read the file afterwards. The server writes JSON on its own.

choices.text: pg_ctlcluster refuses JSON in /var/log/postgresql
choices.why: pg_ctlcluster never sees the format; the plain file is simply not the collector's.

choices.text: Only the logger writes jsonlog
choices.why: Right. logging_collector has context postmaster, and csvlog and jsonlog are written only through it.

choices.text: JSON lines are larger and need a bigger log_rotation_size
choices.why: Rotation size has nothing to do with whether the format can be written at all.

prompt: A monitoring program must count division-by-zero errors across many servers, in several languages of server messages. Which jsonlog field should it match?
hint: Which field is a code rather than English?

choices.text: message
choices.why: "division by zero" is English text, and it is translated when the server's messages are.

choices.text: error_severity
choices.why: ERROR covers every failed statement, not this one kind.

choices.text: backend_type
choices.why: It says a client backend wrote the line, which every client error shares.

choices.text: state_code
choices.why: Right. The SQLSTATE, 22012 here, is the same in every language.

prompt: At 100 transactions a second, around the clock, about how much log would `log_statement = 'all'` write a day, using the lesson's 876 bytes a transaction?
hint: There are 86,400 seconds in a day.

choices.text: About 7.6 GB
choices.why: Right. 876 × 100 × 86,400 is about 7.6 billion bytes, from one setting.

choices.text: About 88 MB
choices.why: That is 876 × 100 × 1,000: a thousand seconds, not a day.

choices.text: About 760 GB
choices.why: A factor of a hundred too many: the multiplication by 100 was done twice.

choices.text: Nothing extra, because pgbench statements are short
choices.why: Short statements are still 125 bytes a line once the prefix is added.

prompt: Users report that a report page "sometimes hangs for a few seconds". With the settings this lesson recommends, which pair of lines would you look for first?
hint: A hang can be a slow statement or a wait behind somebody else.

choices.text: connection received and disconnection
choices.why: They give session length, not why a statement inside it was slow or waiting.

choices.text: checkpoint starting and checkpoint complete
choices.why: Checkpoints can slow a server, but they would not explain one page; look at the page's own statements first.

choices.text: temporary file and STATEMENT
choices.why: A spill is one cause of slowness, but it cannot show a wait; it is the third line to check, not the first.

choices.text: duration, and still waiting
choices.why: Right. The first shows the statement was slow; the second, with its DETAIL, shows whether it was waiting and on whom.

prompt: Which of these take effect with a reload, without a restart? Choose all that apply.
hint: Only one parameter in the lesson needed systemctl restart.

choices.text: log_line_prefix
choices.why: Yes. The reload line itself showed the new value.

choices.text: log_min_duration_statement
choices.why: Yes. pg_reload_conf() was enough.

choices.text: logging_collector
choices.why: It starts a process, so it needs a restart.

choices.text: log_statement
choices.why: Yes. It changed between two logcost.sh runs with a reload.

prompt: A server keeps its log on the same small disk as the data, with Ubuntu's weekly rotation. Somebody enables `log_statement = 'all'` on Monday to debug one application and forgets it. What is the risk by the weekend?
hint: Weekly is a size decision made without looking at the size.

choices.text: logrotate notices the size and rotates early
choices.why: The configuration says weekly with no size or maxsize line; it will not look.

choices.text: The log fills the disk the data lives on
choices.why: Right. Gigabytes a day with no rotation until Sunday, on the data's disk, is lesson 9's full disk arriving through the log.

choices.text: The server switches log_statement off when the disk fills
choices.why: Nothing turns a setting off by itself; the log just keeps growing.

choices.text: Only throughput falls, which the users will notice first
choices.why: On the recording machine throughput did not even change measurably; the disk is the cost that grows.
